final_message:
n `c1_1_1_-2`, up from the parent's 0.398198 (+3.9e-5). It is a refine-lane law. The main risk is time: certification now takes 17.5–18.4 s against the 20 s limit, so a machine about 10% slower would time out and score zero on this instance.

| Item | Parent | New |
|---|---|---|
| Atoms | 64 | 65 |
| Ladder offsets | 4^-j | (2^(L-j) − 1)·u |
| Largest atom denominator | 128 bits | 74 bits |
| Certify time | 16.3–17.6 s | 17.5–18.4 s |
| Strategy time | 2.5 s | 2.6 s |

**Why I stopped here:**
- **Weights are already optimal.** For the 64-atom law with its atoms held fixed, optimizing all weights together gained only 1e-8.
- **Atom count is limited by certification time.** Cost grows with the number of distinct partial sums, about C(K+2,3)·K, and the ladder needs its sums to be distinct. The new offsets remove only about 2.6% of the sums, and the smaller denominators speed certification by about 2%. That is enough for 1 more atom.
- **More atoms would help but do not fit.** Ignoring the time limit, 96 atoms give about 0.39901 and 128 atoms give about 0.39935 (float estimates). 66 atoms take about 19 s and 68 take 20.5 s.

`confidence` returns 0.002: the certified value is 0.0025 below the limit value 0.400695, so it cannot be within 1e-4 of the supremum. `report.json` is `{"c1_1_1_-2": 0.002}`.

I put the 5-line header in `strategy.py`. The question it leaves open is the same as the parent's: whether a law outside the ladder-plus-copy family does better at a fixed atom count.
